value: no significant effect of urban noise (about 65 dB) versus forest-noise control (about 45 dB) on calling when noise was tested in isolation (without urban light)
eye: ear; calling behaviour of wild-caught males under noise playback
method: lab playback on wild-caught males: one baseline night, then two treatment nights with continuous urban or forest noise and a repeated 1-h chorus/rival/silence loop of artificial calls, single-male enclosures; four treatments (Control, Noise, Light, Light + Noise); call number, rate, overlap, complexity, peak-to-peak and RMS amplitude scored
conditions: Wild-caught male tungara frogs (80 collected at six urban and seven forest sites; 45 called in the set-up) housed individually in the lab at STRI facilities in Gamboa, Panama, for at most five nights in September and October 2019, then released at their capture sites. Enclosure 18 x 11.5 x 13 cm inside a 36 x 25 x 58 cm recording box; noise speakers and the call-playback speaker about 25 cm from the enclosure centre. Noise was synthesized from field recordings at four urban and four forest sites and looped continuously: urban noise about 65 dB versus forest noise about 45 dB 'at the center of the enclosure, SPL meter; A weighted, fast, and low' (level stated at a measurement point inside the single frog's enclosure); dB reference not stated. Artificial chorus about 74 dB and rival call (one every 2 s) about 80 dB, so the urban noise lay below the call stimuli. Light: urban 1.3 lx versus forest < 0.01 lx. One baseline night (no noise playbacks, light < 0.01 lx) preceded two treatment nights; the 1-h loop started at 19:00 and calling was recorded until 05:00. Treatments: forest light and forest noise (Control, 13 calling frogs), forest light and urban noise (Noise, 9), urban light and forest noise (Light, 11), urban light and urban noise (Light + Noise, 12); frogs of forest (23) and urban (22) origin. The control is forest-noise playback, not silence. Noise did enter significant or near-significant interactions with light: urban light and noise interacted on RMS amplitude during silence (p = 0.047; Light + Noise +0.7 dB against control, antagonistic, expected additive -5.5 dB), on call complexity during the rival playback (p = 0.02; 17.2% more chucks against 14.0% expected under additivity), near-significantly on peak-to-peak amplitude during the chorus (p = 0.05) and on complexity during the chorus (p = 0.06, antagonistic). Urban light independently of noise raised peak-to-peak amplitude by 4.7 dB during the chorus (p = 0.01). No other light or noise effects on peak-to-peak amplitude (all p > 0.06) or RMS (all p > 0.10); treatment did not affect total calls, call rate or call overlap (all p > 0.08); no other treatment effects on complexity during chorus or silence (all p > 0.35). Origin: urban frogs overlapped the rival more (24.8% vs 12.6%, p = 0.03) and forest frogs called with 24.0% higher complexity during the rival playback (p = 0.01). In the paper's field recordings, call rate tended to increase with noise level (p = 0.05).

source.authors: Smit JAH, Cronin AD, van der Wiel I, Oteman B, Ellers J, Halfwerk W
source.title: Interactive and independent effects of light and noise pollution on sexual signaling in frogs

where: Discussion, subsection 'Impacts of sensory pollutants on calling behavior'
quote: Anthropogenic noise most likely influences signaling via the mechanism of masking, although we did not find a significant impact of noise exposure when tested in isolation.
note: Behavioural null, protocol-specific: noise tested in isolation (Noise vs Control), against a forest-noise playback control, in wild-caught males held in the lab up to five nights; noise is not inert in this paper, since it interacts with urban light (RMS p = 0.047, complexity p = 0.02; see conditions). Abstract: 'Exposure to ALAN alone increased call amplitude,' and 'a combination of ALAN and anthropogenic noise interacted to lead to a higher call complexity' [...]. The quote is the whole Discussion sentence (subsection 'Impacts of sensory pollutants on calling behavior'), read in two abutting pieces on the publisher page; the next sentence begins 'Other studies have shown changes in response to'. Licence sentence read verbatim on the publisher PDF (frontiersin.org): 'This is an open-access article distributed under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution License (CC BY).' Name, family and order from the Amphibian Species of the World page for Engystomops pustulosus (Cope, 1864) (Anura, Leptodactylidae, Leiuperinae), which lists Physalaemus pustulosus among names applied to the species (Lynch 1970) and comments that Wynn and Heyer suggested the North and South American populations meeting in Panama are different species. Species on main for diel, eye_diameter_mm, motion, oil_droplets and pupil_shape, not sense_hearing; DOI not on main.
